background.definition: Laryngitis causes hoarseness and is characterized by acute or chronic inflammation, erythema, and edema of the laryngeal mucosa.

list.listitem: Common—acute laryngitis diagnosed in 1.8% of ambulatory office visits (NAMCS 1975-1976).
Chronic laryngitis is 5.5 cases per 1000 persons per year based on 1983 to 1985 NHANES data.
$112 billion in 1997
Viral illness (e.g., rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus, coxsackie, coronavirus, RSV)
Respiratory allergies
Voice abuse
Gastroesophageal reflux
Irritants
Benign neoplasms
Other infectious agents
Stress
Laryngeal malignancy
Hypothyroidism
Vocal cord paralysis (nerve injury or neuromuscular disease)
Mucosal inflammation leads to edema of the vocal cords.
This edema and thickening of the cords decreases their ability to vibrate, affecting phonation and causing hoarseness.
Patients typically present with hoarseness, usually accompanied by other symptoms of viral URI. C
Laryngoscopy with possible biopsy is recommended if hoarseness persists beyond 2 to 3 weeks, especially with risk factors for cancer (e.g., tobacco, alcohol, marijuana, occupational chemicals). C
Patients typically present with hoarseness, usually accompanied by other symptoms of viral URI.
Quality of the hoarseness may aid in diagnosis.
Laryngoscopy, if done, shows mild erythema of vocal cords.
Chronic laryngitis is often associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), but GERD is rarely the sole cause.
More commonly GERD is considered an aggravating co-factor.
Diagnostic testing is generally not needed unless prolonged course leads to suspicion of causes of hoarseness other than acute viral laryngitis.

Direct and indirect laryngoscopy to visualize vocal cords is recommended if hoarseness persists more than 2 to 3 weeks, particularly in a patient with risk factors for cancer such as smoking, chewing tobacco use, or heavy alcohol use.
No data are available on sensitivity or specificity of these tests.
If course of illness is typical of upper respiratory viral illness, examination of cords is not usually needed.

After voice rest and local care measures for 2 to 3 weeks, if symptoms persist, consider viewing the vocal cords (direct or indirect laryngoscopy), particularly if risk factors for neoplasia are present.
Antibiotics are not effective in acute laryngitis. B
Saline nasal irrigation may be helpful. B
Try speech therapy if symptoms are prolonged (and there are no risk factors for neoplasia) before proceeding to laryngoscopy. C
Antibiotics are not effective in acute laryngitis.

A meta-analysis identified 2 RCTs: one of 100 patients randomized to penicillin or placebo and the other with 106 patients randomized to erythromycin to placebo. There was no clinically important benefit seen in either study.

When laryngitis is associated with GERD, called laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), empiric proton pump inhibitor therapy for 2 to 4 months did not significantly achieve a 50% reduction in patient-reported laryngeal symptoms. However, a subsequent meta-analysis found some benefit from antireflux surgery and longer duration (>8 weeks) medical therapy.
Speech therapy may help if vocal abuse is cause or in patients with recurrent episodes of laryngitis.
Speech therapy may also help patients with a slow resolution of an otherwise typical viral episode.
In croup, humidified air is minimally effective.
A Cochrane review found low quality evidence for the effectiveness of saline nasal irrigation for acute upper respiratory tract infections, including laryngitis.
Voice rest is generally recommended, though no studies of improved outcomes are available.
Vocal hygiene, including oral hydration and avoidance of drugs that cause mucosal drying, such as antihistamines, seems reasonable.
Avoidance of known respiratory irritants is recommended. These include tobacco, alcohol, marijuana, and occupational chemical exposure.
If you are unable to visualize the larynx to rule out neoplasia in patients with risk factors or persistence of symptoms, a referral for laryngoscopy is appropriate.
Symptoms usually resolve without specific treatment in a few days to a week. B
